**On the Hour Before Anyone Wakes**

There's a particular quality to the world at 5:47 a.m., before the day has committed to anything. The light hasn't decided what color it will be—it hovers in that gray-blue ambiguity where streetlamps still glow but no longer matter. Coffee makers wait. Birds rehearse.

I've always thought this hour belongs to a different species of time than the rest of the day. Noon is loud with purpose; midnight carries its own reputation. But the pre-dawn hour is unclaimed territory. Nothing is expected of it. The day has not yet begun keeping score.

In kitchens across every city, someone stands barefoot on cold tile, waiting for water to boil, watching steam rise like a small apology from the kettle. They are, in that moment, neither yesterday's failures nor tomorrow's ambitions—just a person and a mug and the hum of the refrigerator holding its one long note.

Maybe that's why insomniacs and early risers share a certain knowing look, like members of a secret society. They've seen the backstage of the day. They know the streets before traffic gives them meaning, the houses as shapes rather than addresses, the sky as potential rather than forecast.

By 6:30, the spell breaks. Alarms fire. Trains shudder awake. The world puts on its costume and resumes the performance. But somewhere, the memory lingers—that brief window when everything was still possible because nothing had started yet, when the whole day lay folded and unworn, smelling faintly of coffee and rain.
